venues.d: A 1787 villa above the water that the world voted its finest — and it wears the crown lightly.
A Renaissance cardinal's villa turned hotel since 1873 — the grande dame the whole lake is measured against.
A 1910 Art Nouveau palace facing Bellagio, with a pool that floats on the lake itself.
A neoclassical estate of nine villas in a centuries-old botanical park — the group's precision on the quiet eastern shore.
Patricia Urquiola's cool, modern lakehouse — the design-led answer to the lake's old palaces.
A Belle Époque palace at the very tip of Bellagio, looking down both arms of the lake.
An 1858 palazzo above the ferry quay — Como town's only lakefront five-star, intimate and jewel-like.
Soprano Giuditta Pasta's lakeside estate reborn as a villa resort — a floating spa and gardens on the eastern shore.
A crisp modern hotel on a quiet, ferry-light stretch — glass, water and an uninterrupted view.
An 1860s villa on the water between Como town and Cernobbio — a graceful, well-placed lakeside base.
A Renaissance villa and terraced botanical gardens dropping to the water on the lake's loveliest village.
A reborn lakefront grande dame on the western shore, with one of the lake's largest spas.
A small, all-suite villa retreat with its own lido on the eastern shore — quietly exclusive.
A design-forward hilltop hotel with an infinity pool over the lake's most scenic middle reach.
A restored 19th-century villa estate with a private beach on the wilder eastern shore.
A polished small hotel with a lake pool on the discreet western shore near Laglio.
A family-run hillside hotel above Bellagio with gardens, a pool and the whole lake below.
A landmark lakefront hotel on Bellagio's waterfront square — right where the ferries dock.
Ettore Bocchia's molecular Mediterranean cooking at the very tip of Bellagio — the lake's grandest dining room.
Raffaele Lenzi's lake-and-Valtellina cooking on Il Sereno's arched terrace — modern, precise, deeply of the lake.
Davide Caranchini's herb-and-foraging kitchen — the lake's most progressive cooking, from a Noma-trained mind.
A confident, contemporary kitchen that quietly holds the star for Como town itself.
The only table in the world serving the maestro's canon — the gold-leaf risotto, on the lake's most beautiful terrace.
Italian tradition with a Japanese nuance, set in the resort's botanical park — bright and considered.
A rooftop dining room over Como town, the lake spreading south — the town's most glamorous table.
Lake-facing Italian cooking within the lake's grandest palace hotel — polished and generous.
Grand-hotel dining in Villa d'Este's frescoed halls — old-world ceremony at the lake's most storied address.
A lakeside terrace at Bellagio's northern point, cooking the lake's own freshwater fish.
A lake-terrace restaurant between Como and Cernobbio — gracious Italian cooking over the water.
A family fishermen's institution serving the lake's own catch, hauled in that morning.
A warm village trattoria off Cernobbio's square — regional Lombard cooking done properly.
A tucked-away osteria in old Como serving honest Comasco plates and local wine.
A grand-café dining room on Como's lakefront piazza — classic Italian with the promenade at your feet.
A lakeside 'crotto' on the western shore — the old cave-cellar tradition, turned refined.
A lake-terrace kitchen on a quiet eastern stretch, cooking the day's freshwater catch.
A pretty lakeside square-side room near the Comacina island — Italian cooking with a view of the water.
An honest lakeside kitchen on the western shore — freshwater fish and Lombard classics without ceremony.
A waterside bar-kitchen on Bellagio's shore — simple plates, aperitivo and the lake at eye level.

The most cinematic house on the lake, standing alone on a wooded promontory with its famous loggia and sculpted terraces cascading to the water. A Star Wars and James Bond backdrop, and one of Como's most coveted wedding stages, so arrive by private taxi-boat from Lido di Lenno and book the interior tour well ahead.

A 17th-century villa wrapped in eight hectares of botanical garden that turns incandescent in spring, when hundreds of azaleas and rhododendrons bloom at once. Inside are Canova sculptures and marble halls; families can wander the fern valley, bamboo grove and citrus terraces at an unhurried pace.

Napoleonic-era gardens sweeping along the Bellagio waterfront, planted with camellias, ancient plane trees and Egyptian statuary, with a Japanese pond and a lakeside path made for a slow morning. Only the gardens and chapel open to visitors, which keeps the crowds thin and the mood serene.

A former convent turned lakeside residence, its two-kilometre botanical garden threaded with cypresses, agaves and lemon houses running right along the water toward Fiumelatte. The richly furnished house-museum shows how Como's aristocracy actually lived, a rewarding pairing for multi-generational visits.

The legendary 18-hectare park crowning the Bellagio promontory, owned by the Rockefeller Foundation and reachable only on a guided walk that climbs through cypress avenues and olive groves to panoramas over both arms of the lake. Tours leave from the Promobellagio tower; wear proper shoes for the uphill first hour.

Four centuries in the making, Como's Gothic-Renaissance cathedral rises straight off the old town's marble streets, its facade carved with saints and, unusually, the two Roman Plinys. Entry is free and the cool, tapestry-hung nave is a fine first stop before the lakefront promenade.

A seven-minute vintage funicular, running since 1894, that hoists you from the lakefront to the hilltop village of Brunate for a sweeping view over Como and, on clear days, the Alps and Monte Rosa. A short, easy outing that older travellers and children both love; buy tickets ahead in summer.

Como has spun and printed silk for the world's great fashion houses for generations, and this museum walks you through the full craft, from cocoon to finished bolt, with the old dyeing and printing machinery on display. A quiet, tactile counterpoint to the villas, and useful context before shopping the city's silk ateliers.

A grand neoclassical mansion of 1780 set in a lakeside park at the edge of Como town, its formal gardens and waterfront lawns open year-round and free to stroll. The interiors host rotating exhibitions when not under restoration; the park alone is a graceful place to breathe between town and lake.

Fourteen Baroque chapels climb a hillside above the western shore, filled with life-size terracotta figures telling the Mysteries of the Rosary, ending at a hilltop sanctuary framed by olive groves and views to Isola Comacina. Peaceful, free and open at all hours, it rewards travellers who want depth beyond the villa circuit.

The lake's only island, inhabited since Roman times and razed in medieval war, now a green archaeological haven with church ruins and a single storied restaurant reached by taxi-boat. A short, atmospheric crossing that pairs beautifully with a long lunch and a private boat waiting to collect you.

venues.n: Private boat tour of the lake
venues.d: The definitive way to read Lake Como: a chartered wooden Venetian-style motorboat with your own skipper, gliding past Villa del Balbianello, Villa Oleandra and the Bellagio promontory while you set the pace and the aperitivo. Discreet, flexible and ideal for a family or a honeymoon afternoon on the water.

A short, red-railed promenade cantilevered over the water, linking Varenna's ferry pier to its old town past flower baskets and painted houses with Vezio Castle above. Free, gentle and unabashedly romantic, it is the classic first stroll of a Como honeymoon.

A thousand-year-old watchtower castle on the ridge above Varenna, reached by a steep twenty-minute climb and rewarded with one of the widest views on the lake, plus falconry displays in season. Bring water and good shoes; the panorama down to the Bellagio fork is worth the effort.

A dramatic gorge where two streams plunge into the lake beside the arched Ponte della Civera, a scene so striking Leonardo da Vinci noted it in his Codex Atlanticus. Best framed from the little Romanesque bridge, reached by a stairway down through the tiered village; approach by boat for the finest angle.

One of the largest and most opulent private villas on the lake, its baroque terraces and frescoed rooms familiar from House of Gucci, now available for exclusive private visits, events and stays. A true behind-the-gates experience for those who want the lake's grandeur to themselves.

An easy 11-kilometre lakeside walking route following the ancient Roman Via Regina through six villages, past Romanesque churches, hidden coves and the gates of the great villas. Walk it in linked stages at your own rhythm, then be met by a driver or boat at the next hamlet.

The "pearl of the lake": steep cobbled stairways lined with silk shops, gelaterie and cafes, spilling toward the point where the lake's two arms meet. The most photographed village on Como, best enjoyed early or in the evening once the day boats have gone.

A tumble of ochre and terracotta houses on the quieter eastern shore, with a tiny fishing harbour, a piazza church and a slower, more intimate mood than Bellagio across the water. An ideal base for couples who want beauty without the crush.

A lively lakeside town with a broad promenade, an elegant central piazza and easy ferries across to Bellagio and Varenna, forming the third point of the lake's "golden triangle." Its road over to Lugano makes it a natural launch point for a Swiss day.

A graceful stretch of western shore anchored by the belle-epoque Grand Hotel Tremezzo and its floating lake pool, with lush lakeside gardens and Villa Carlotta next door. The register here is unhurried old-world luxury, perfect for a leisurely lunch by the water.

venues.n: Lenno and the Zoca de l'Oli
venues.d: A sheltered, sun-trapped bay ringed by olive groves, the launch point for taxi-boats to Villa del Balbianello and a calm spot for a swim from Lido di Lenno. Gentle and family-friendly, with an easy lakeside promenade and simple trattorie.

A tiny, little-visited fishing village of stone stairways just up the eastern shore from Como, home to the romantic ruined-glamour of Villa Pliniana with its intermittent spring and 70-metre waterfall. A quiet detour for travellers who prefer discovery to crowds.

An aristocratic little town at the southern end of the western shore, defined by the legendary Villa d'Este hotel and a genteel lakeside piazza of cafes and boutiques. The most discreetly grand address on the lower lake, and an easy first stop out of Como.

The 19th-century estate where director Luchino Visconti spent his summers, its neo-Renaissance villa and lakeside park now a cultural and event venue with cinematic atmosphere. Best seen when an exhibition or the gardens are open; a fitting stop for lovers of film and design.

A short cable car from Lecco lifts you to a high alpine balcony facing the Resegone, with meadow trails, a rifugio lunch and cool air well above the lake. A quick nature escape that gives grandparents and children an easy taste of the mountains.

venues.n: Seaplane flight with Aero Club Como
venues.d: Take off from the water at the world's oldest seaplane club, founded in 1930, for a roughly half-hour flight banking over Bellagio, Villa del Balbianello and the villa-lined shores. A genuinely rare thrill and an unforgettable family or honeymoon splurge; book ahead in high season.

One of the lake's prettiest and most vertical hamlets, its stone houses stacked down to the famous gorge and Roman-medieval bridge. A photogenic, off-the-beaten-track pause for those exploring the wilder eastern shore by boat or car.

A brooding 16th-century villa built over an intermittent spring described by Pliny two thousand years ago, once a retreat for Napoleon, Byron and Rossini, and now an exclusive private estate. A romantic, faintly gothic landmark best appreciated from the water or on a private visit.

Como remains Europe's silk capital, and its ateliers and outlets sell scarves, ties and fabrics woven for the world's fashion maisons at the source. A refined, easily veg-friendly afternoon of shopping paired with an aperitivo on the Como lakefront.

Italy's shortest river, a milky-white torrent that gushes only from spring to autumn then mysteriously vanishes, a curiosity Leonardo da Vinci himself tried to explain. A short, easy walk from Varenna to a small, atmospheric natural wonder.

Under an hour by train from Como, Milan opens the Duomo, the Galleria's fashion arcades, Leonardo's Last Supper and the world's great luxury boutiques. A perfect contrast day for shopping and art, best paired with a private driver for door-to-door ease.

A walled hilltop old town of Venetian ramparts, piazzas and a funicular, remarkably intact and far quieter than Milan, reached in about an hour and a half. A rewarding half-day of history and long lunches for those who have already done the lake's headline sights.

venues.n: Valtellina wine and mountains day trip
venues.d: North of the lake, the steep terraced vineyards of Valtellina produce elegant Nebbiolo reds like Sassella and Inferno, tasted at family cellars amid alpine scenery and hearty local cheeses. A characterful excursion for wine lovers who want the lake's mountainous, gastronomic hinterland.

Even without a room, a lunch or aperitivo at the fabled Villa d'Este lets you walk its 25 acres of Renaissance gardens, the mosaic nymphaeum and the floating pool on the lake. The lake's grandest hotel and a benchmark of discreet, old-money luxury.

Beneath the Sacro Monte, a small museum tells the story of vanished Isola Comacina and the surrounding shore, while the Romanesque bell tower of Santa Maria Maddalena stands out for its unusual gothic crown. A quiet cultural pairing for the UNESCO climb above.

A private early-evening boat charter when the light turns gold on the mountains and the villa windows catch fire, glass in hand as the lake empties of day-trippers. Quietly the most romantic hour on Como, easily arranged with a skipper and a picnic hamper.

A genteel resort hamlet on the western shore, home to a rare English church and the woodland path up to the panoramic San Martino chapel high above the lake. A gentle, storied stretch of shore favoured historically by British and German visitors seeking calm.
A rooftop terrace over Como town, the lake stretching south — the town's most glamorous sundowner.
A drink in the frescoed grandeur of the lake's most storied villa-hotel — old-world ceremony at its most complete.
An Art Nouveau bar facing Bellagio, with the floating pool below and the whole lake in the glass.
A quiet drink on the terrace of the world's most-decorated boutique villa — the calmest luxury on the lake.
Patricia Urquiola's cool lakehouse bar — modern, low-lit and precise, a design-world nightcap on the water.
